newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal vote hit by confusion, opposition cries foul.
newsitem.headline: Nepal vote hit by confusion, opposition cries foul.

text.p: Nepal's parliament was thrown into confusion on Monday as the opposition disrupted proceedings on a no-confidence motion against the government, alleging that the ruling coalition had forcibly kept away its supporters.

Confusion reigned in the Himalayan kingdom after six hours of debate on Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's 15-month-old centre-right coalition when communists complained that some of their key supporters had vanished.

They said five government ministers and one deputy each from two minor parties, the Nepal Workers and Peasants Party (NWPP) and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP) were kept away by the government for fear that they would vote against it.

"Without a minister's reply about the information on the missing ministers and the members, the business of the house cannot proceed," said Khadga Prasad Oli, deputy of the main opposition Unified Marxist Leninist (UML) party.
The vote was expected to take place late on Monday or on Tuesday.
The speaker held discussions with opposition leaders to end a stalemate that followed an adjournment of the lower house, but the house was adjourned again twice after 8.45 p.m. (1515 GMT).

The speaker announced that debate was over and reconvened the house at 9.30 p.m., when Deuba was expected to reply to the debate. But opposition deputies squatted near the speaker's podium and did not allow the house to function, witnesses said.

The NWPP announced earlier in the day that its three deputies would vote against the government. The chief of the NSP is a member of the government, but two remaining deputies of his party had said they would vote against the coalition.
"One of my three deputies is missing since the morning from his residence," said NWPP's president, Narayan Man Bijukuchhe.

"Five ministers were sent to Bangkok for fear that they will vote against the government," said former minister Kamal Thapa of the Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), who resigned from the coalition last week to campaign against the government.
Deuba denied any wrongdoing and said the ministers had gone to Bangkok for medical treatment.
"No one has been kidnapped and I am ready to retire from politics if it is proved that the government has kidnapped anyone," he told parliament.
"I have authorised the ministers to go to Bangkok for medical treatment," Deuba said.
Constituents of the coalition are divided over support for the government.
NWPP's support for the no-confidence motion, moved on Saturday by the UML, had increased the chances that the government will lose a close-run vote, politicians said.
Deuba's three party coalition commands 108 seats in a house of 205 members. Of this, Deuba's Nepali Congress has 86 member and the RPP, 19 members. But the RPP is sharply divided.
Politicians estimated that the decision by NWPP will raise the number of votes in support of the motion to 104, just above the 103 votes required to pass it.

Deuba's Nepali Congress was demanding disqualification of the two defecting NSP members. If it succeeded the opposition will lose two crucial votes. But one of the two NSP members was not present in the house, and this sparked protests.
